title: A park is more than a pause
hook: How do you notice a public place without making its users the attraction?

blocks.heading: Hook
blocks.text: You can visit a park as a gap between attractions, or as a place worth paying attention to itself. Put the checklist aside for a few minutes. What changes when you notice the relationship between a path, a bench and a patch of shade, rather than looking for the next photograph?

blocks.heading: Context
blocks.text: The Huangpu district account published by Shanghai’s government traces Fuxing Park’s opening to 1909 under the name Gujiazhai Park. It describes French-style garden design and features including a rose garden, a pond and a rockery. This is historical and landscape context, not a promise that every feature or gate is accessible today.

blocks.heading: Human perspective
blocks.text: A park’s users do not owe visitors an explanation of their lives. No resident’s opinion is quoted in this story. Your own experience can be modest and still meaningful: perhaps you discover that sitting quietly tells you more about how you travel than another rushed stop would have done. Other visitors may come away differently.

blocks.heading: Look closer
blocks.text: If current access allows, choose a public path and notice one design detail. Where can someone stop without blocking movement? What does the layout encourage you to see? Keep photographs focused on space and objects; seek consent before photographing identifiable people. Do not join an activity uninvited or assume an occupied corner is a performance.

blocks.heading: Go deeper
blocks.text: Use the observation card for a short, optional visit. Check VDC and official information for current entry conditions, and choose a different permitted public space if the park is closed or crowded. Before leaving, write down one observation and one unanswered question. Learning to separate them is a useful way to carry curiosity into the rest of the city.
